# Deployment {background-color="#2E6E8E"}

## Two pieces, two homes

Your final project is **two processes** — they deploy separately and find each other by URL:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.patches as mp
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9.5, 3.4))
ax.add_patch(mp.FancyBboxPatch((0.3, 0.7), 3.4, 1.6, boxstyle="round,pad=0.1", fc="#EAF2F6", ec="#2E6E8E"))
ax.text(2.0, 1.7, "Streamlit client", ha="center", fontsize=11, fontweight="bold")
ax.text(2.0, 1.15, "Streamlit Community Cloud\n(from your GitHub repo)", ha="center", fontsize=9)
ax.add_patch(mp.FancyBboxPatch((6.1, 0.7), 3.4, 1.6, boxstyle="round,pad=0.1", fc="#2E6E8E", ec="#2E6E8E"))
ax.text(7.8, 1.7, "FastAPI model server", ha="center", fontsize=11, fontweight="bold", color="white")
ax.text(7.8, 1.15, "any host that runs uvicorn\n(Render / Railway / a VM)", ha="center", fontsize=9, color="white")
ax.annotate("", xy=(6.0, 1.5), xytext=(3.8, 1.5), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", lw=2, color="#d9534f"))
ax.text(4.9, 1.75, "API_URL (config!)", ha="center", fontsize=10, color="#d9534f")
ax.set_xlim(0, 9.9); ax.set_ylim(0.3, 2.7); ax.axis("off")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The #1 deployment bug in this course's history-to-be: a client hard-coded to `127.0.0.1:8000`. Works on your laptop, dead on the web.

## Configuration, not hard-coding

```python
# client: read the server location from config
API_URL = st.secrets.get("API_URL",
          os.getenv("API_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8000"))   # local fallback
```

- Secrets/keys → `st.secrets` or environment variables — **never the repo**
- `requirements.txt` pins what both pieces need
- README says how to run each piece — your grader follows it verbatim

::: {.gw-box}
**Reproducibility = someone else can run it.** That someone is me, during grading.
:::

## The deployment checklist {.smaller}

```text
[ ] requirements.txt pins all dependencies (both pieces)
[ ] No secrets committed (st.secrets / env vars)
[ ] Server has /health; starts clean from the README
[ ] Client reads API_URL from config (not localhost)
[ ] Client degrades gracefully when the server is down
[ ] README: how to run, how to test, where it's deployed
```

We run this list live in Block 2, on a real project.

# Ethics: charts people believe {background-color="#2E6E8E"}

## The course's honesty lessons, in one place {.smaller}

You've met every chart crime already — by modality:

- **Time** (Wk 4): truncated axes, silent smoothing, dual axes
- **Maps** (Wk 9): counts as rates, undisclosed classification, area-distorting projections
- **Networks** (Wk 6): hairballs that perform insight
- **Text** (Wk 7): word clouds as evidence
- **Models** (Wk 13): the confident progress bar on a 50/50 prediction

The common thread: each one **borrows the authority of data** to say more than the data says.

## The authority problem

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(11)
months = np.arange(1, 13)
vals = 100 + np.cumsum(rng.normal(0.3, 1.2, 12))
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.6))
axes[0].plot(months, vals, color="#d9534f", lw=2)
axes[0].set_ylim(vals.min()-0.5, vals.max()+0.5)
axes[0].set_title("'SURGING' — truncated, no context")
axes[1].plot(months, vals, color="#2E6E8E", lw=2)
axes[1].set_ylim(0, vals.max()*1.15)
axes[1].set_title("Same data, zero baseline: ~3% drift")
for a in axes: a.set_xlabel("month")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

A polished chart *looks* objective — that's precisely its persuasive power, and your responsibility. Especially when the thing visualized is **a model's opinion** that users will over-trust.

## Accessibility is part of honesty {.smaller}

A chart that ~5% of your audience cannot decode isn't done:

- **Colorblind-safe palettes** (`sns.set_palette("colorblind")`, viridis family)
- Never meaning by color **alone** — add markers, labels, direct annotation
- Alt text on images (`st.image(..., caption=...)`); real labels on controls
- Contrast that survives a projector

::: {.gw-box}
Final-project rubric line item — and a Block 3 critique lens.
:::

## The workshop: how critique works {.smaller}

Block 3: **2–3 minute lightning demo** each, then structured peer critique:

```text
1 thing that works  ·  1 thing that's unclear  ·  1 concrete suggestion
```

Four lenses, in order: **accuracy/honesty → clarity/focus → the client–server loop (does it work? fail gracefully?) → accessibility.**

Critique the work, not the person; receive it with notes, not defenses. You'll use every minute of feedback before the deadline.

## Discussion {.gw-discussion}

**1.** Your model is 70% accurate but your app's polish makes it *feel* authoritative. What design choices would honestly communicate "useful but fallible"?

**2.** What did "visualizing complex data" turn out to mean — what would you tell yourself in Week 1?
